authoredSolutions.31: In a nucleic acid chain, the \(3'\)-OH of the sugar of one nucleotide is joined to the \(5'\)-OH of the sugar of the next nucleotide through a phosphate unit. Because the same phosphate forms TWO ester bonds (one to each sugar), the link is called a phosphodiester linkage. A glycosidic linkage joins a base to the sugar (nucleoside formation), a peptide linkage joins amino acids, and a disulphide linkage joins two cysteine residues. Hence the correct answer is (A).
authoredSolutions.32: The four options are (A) cyclohexane-1,3-dione, (B) cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione, (C) cyclohexane-1,4-dione and (D) cyclohexane-1,2,3-trione. Complete enolisation of cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione converts all three C=O groups into C-OH groups and generates 1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene (phloroglucinol), which is AROMATIC. Aromatic stabilisation of the enol form is far larger than the conjugation/intramolecular hydrogen bonding available to a simple \(\beta\)-diketone, so the equilibrium lies almost completely on the enol side. Cyclohexane-1,4-dione has no \(\alpha\)-carbon flanked by two carbonyls at all. Hence (B) shows the highest enol content.
authoredSolutions.33: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and has no accessible \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell (\(n = 2\)), so it cannot expand its octet or be oxidised by any other element. It therefore shows only the \(-1\) oxidation state (and \(0\) in \(F_{2}\)). Chlorine, bromine and iodine all have vacant \(d\)-orbitals and show \(-1, +1, +3, +5, +7\). Hence the element not showing a variable oxidation state is fluorine, option (D).
authoredSolutions.34: The options are (A) aniline, (B) diphenylamine, (C) pyrrole and (D) pyrrolidine. In aniline and diphenylamine the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring(s), so basicity falls (diphenylamine, with two rings, is weaker still). In pyrrole the lone pair is part of the aromatic \(6\pi\) sextet; donating it would destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole is essentially non-basic. In pyrrolidine the nitrogen is \(sp^{3}\) hybridised, saturated and carries a fully localised lone pair, with two electron-releasing alkyl groups. Hence pyrrolidine is the strongest Bronsted base, option (D).
authoredSolutions.35:
Fill each \(d\)-subshell by Hund's rule and count unpaired electrons \(n\), then use \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\) B.M.
\(3d^{7}\): \(n = 3\), \(\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\)
\(3d^{8}\): \(n = 2\), \(\mu = \sqrt{8} = 2.83\)
\(3d^{3}\): \(n = 3\), \(\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\)
\(3d^{6}\): \(n = 4\), \(\mu = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\)
The maximum number of unpaired electrons (4) occurs for \(3d^{6}\), so \([Ar]3d^{6}\) has the highest magnetic moment, option (D).
authoredSolutions.36: The options are (A) hexane-2,3-dione, (B) hexane-2,5-dione, (C) hexan-3-one and (D) hexane-2,4-dione. Only in (D) is a \(CH_{2}\) group flanked by TWO carbonyls, i.e. a \(\beta\)-diketone. The carbanion left after removing that hydrogen is delocalised over both carbonyl oxygens, so its \(pK_{a}\) is about \(9\), against about \(19{-}20\) for the \(\alpha\)-hydrogen of a simple ketone (C) or of a 1,4-diketone (B); in the 1,2-diketone (A) the two carbonyls are adjacent and cannot both stabilise the same carbanion. Hence hexane-2,4-dione has the most acidic hydrogen, option (D).
authoredSolutions.37: A negative deviation means the A-B interactions in the mixture are STRONGER than the average of the A-A and B-B interactions. Molecules therefore escape into the vapour less readily, so the observed vapour pressure is LOWER than that predicted by Raoult's law. Since a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, a lowered vapour pressure means a HIGHER temperature is needed, i.e. the boiling point is raised (such mixtures form maximum-boiling azeotropes). Hence decreased vapour pressure and increased boiling point, option (D).

Find the oxidation state, the \(d\)-count and the number of unpaired electrons \(n\), then \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\).
\(P = [FeF_{6}]^{3-}\): \(Fe^{3+} = 3d^{5}\); \(F^{-}\) is a weak-field ligand, so high spin, \(n = 5\), \(\mu = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\) B.M.
\(Q = [V(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}\): \(V^{2+} = 3d^{3}\), \(n = 3\), \(\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\) B.M.
\(R = [Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}\): \(Fe^{2+} = 3d^{6}\); \(H_{2}O\) is weak field, so high spin \(t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}\), \(n = 4\), \(\mu = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\) B.M.
Increasing order: \(Q(3.87) < R(4.90) < P(5.92)\), option (C).
authoredSolutions.39: \(CCl_{4}\) is tetrahedral and the four identical \(C-Cl\) bond moments cancel exactly, so \(\mu = 0\). \(CO_{2}\) is linear and the two \(C=O\) moments are equal and opposite, so \(\mu = 0\). \(CH_{2}=CH_{2}\) is planar and symmetric with only weakly polar \(C-H\) bonds, so \(\mu = 0\). In \(CHCl_{3}\) one \(Cl\) of the tetrahedron has been replaced by \(H\), destroying the symmetry, so the three \(C-Cl\) moments no longer cancel and a net dipole (\(\mu \approx 1.04\) D) results. Hence \(CHCl_{3}\) is polar, option (D).

Statement I is TRUE: the \(4f\) (lanthanoids) and \(5f\) (actinoids) series each contain 14 elements whose properties are nearly identical; placing them in the main body would stretch the table and break the principle that elements in a group must resemble one another, so they are shown separately at the bottom.
Statement II is FALSE: \(s\)-block elements (alkali and alkaline earth metals) are extremely reactive, reacting readily with air and water, and are therefore NEVER found in the free/pure state in nature - they occur only as compounds (halides, carbonates, sulphates, silicates).
Statement I true, Statement II false, option (C).
authoredSolutions.41:
Statement II is clearly FALSE: Lucas reagent (conc. \(HCl + ZnCl_{2}\)) gives immediate turbidity only with tertiary alcohols; ethanol is primary and gives no turbidity at room temperature (it needs heating).
Statement I is taken as FALSE: for the nitrophenols the standard order taught is \(o\)-nitrophenol \(>\) \(p\)-nitrophenol \(>\) \(m\)-nitrophenol, the ortho isomer being made strongly acidic by the proximity \(-I\) effect in addition to the \(-R\) effect. So \(p\)-nitrophenol is NOT more acidic than the ortho isomer, and the claim fails.
Both statements false, option (C).
authoredSolutions.42:
The five compounds are (a) \(Bu-OH\), (b) \(p\)-nitrophenol, (c) \(p\)-methoxyphenol, (d) phenol, (e) 2,4-dinitrophenol.
An alcohol is by far the weakest acid because its conjugate base (alkoxide) has no delocalisation and the alkyl group is electron releasing (\(pK_{a} \approx 16\)). All the phenols are much more acidic because the phenoxide is resonance stabilised (\(pK_{a} \approx 10\)).
Among the phenols, the electron-releasing \(-OCH_{3}\) group destabilises the phenoxide, so \(p\)-methoxyphenol (\(pK_{a} \approx 10.2\)) is slightly weaker than phenol (\(10.0\)). One \(-NO_{2}\) group at para withdraws electrons by \(-I\) and \(-R\), giving \(p\)-nitrophenol (\(7.15\)); two nitro groups make 2,4-dinitrophenol strongest (\(4.1\)).
Ascending acidity: \((a) < (c) < (d) < (b) < (e)\), which is option (D).
authoredSolutions.43:
Assertion is correct: boron melts at \(2453\) K, far above the other group 13 elements (\(Al\) 933 K, \(Ga\) 303 K).
Reason is correct AND explains it: boron is not a normal metal - it is a covalent network solid built from icosahedral \(B_{12}\) units linked by strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice. Melting therefore requires breaking a three-dimensional covalent network, not merely a metallic lattice, which demands a very high temperature. Hence both correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), option (B).
authoredSolutions.44: Cyclohexene (figure image25) is a six-membered CARBOCYCLIC ring, so it is not acyclic. It contains only one \(C=C\) double bond, so it has neither a benzene ring (not benzenoid) nor a closed conjugated \(4n+2\) \(\pi\) system (not aromatic). A cyclic, non-aromatic hydrocarbon of this type is classified as ALICYCLIC (aliphatic-cyclic). Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.45:
Lead(II) oxide/hydroxide is amphoteric, so yellow \(PbCrO_{4}\) dissolves in hot alkali:
\[PbCrO_{4} + 4NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}[Pb(OH)_{4}] + Na_{2}CrO_{4}\]
The lead-containing product is the tetrahydroxidoplumbate(II) ion \([Pb(OH)_{4}]^{2-}\). Its charge is \(+2 + 4(-1) = -2\), so it is DIANIONIC, and four \(OH^{-}\) ligands are attached, so the coordination number is FOUR. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.46:
Ammonium carbonate \((NH_{4})_{2}CO_{3}\) is the salt of a weak acid \((H_{2}CO_{3}, K_{a_{1}} = 4.3 \times 10^{-7})\) and a weak base \((NH_{4}OH, K_{b} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5})\). For such a salt
\[pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}\left(pK_{a} - pK_{b}\right)\]
Here \(K_{b} > K_{a}\), so \(pK_{a} > pK_{b}\) and \(pH > 7\): the solution is basic. Statement I is therefore correct, and Statement II states exactly the general rule that decides it, so it is correct too. Both statements correct, option (A).

The figure (image26) shows a cyclohexane ring bearing two methyl groups on one carbon and an ethyl group two carbons away (a 1,1-dimethyl-3-ethyl pattern).
Rules: substituent prefixes are cited in ALPHABETICAL order (ethyl before methyl, and 'dimethyl' alphabetises under m), while the LOCANTS are chosen to be the lowest set, which is \(\{1,1,3\}\). Numbering from the gem-dimethyl carbon gives methyls at C1, C1 and ethyl at C3.
Writing the prefixes alphabetically with those locants gives 3-Ethyl-1,1-dimethylcyclohexane, option (B). Option (D) has the right locants but cites methyl before ethyl; options (A) and (C) use a higher locant set.

This is the chromyl chloride test for chloride:
\[4NaCl + K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7} + 6H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 2CrO_{2}Cl_{2} + 4NaHSO_{4} + 2KHSO_{4} + 3H_{2}O\]
The reddish-brown fumes (B) are chromyl chloride \(CrO_{2}Cl_{2}\). Passing them into \(NaOH\) gives the yellow chromate solution (C):
\[CrO_{2}Cl_{2} + 4NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}CrO_{4} + 2NaCl + 2H_{2}O\]
So (B) \(= CrO_{2}Cl_{2}\) and (C) \(= Na_{2}CrO_{4}\), option (A). Note that the pair is asked 'respectively' - option (B) has the same two species in the reversed order and is a trap.

\(S_{N}1\) proceeds through a planar \(sp^{2}\) carbocation intermediate that the nucleophile can attack equally from either face, giving both enantiomers - i.e. RACEMISATION (in practice partial, with slight inversion excess).
\(S_{N}2\) is a one-step backside attack; the nucleophile enters \(180^{\circ}\) opposite the leaving group, so the configuration at the stereocentre is turned inside out - INVERSION (Walden inversion).
Hence racemisation in \(S_{N}1\) and inversion in \(S_{N}2\), option (D).

Neodymium has \(Z = 60\). Xenon accounts for 54 electrons, leaving 6 to place. Neodymium is the fourth member of the \(4f\) (lanthanoid) series, and after \(La\), \(Ce\), \(Pr\) the \(4f\) subshell fills steadily while the \(6s\) subshell stays full. Hence
\[Nd: [Xe]4f^{4}6s^{2}\]
Option (B) uses \(5f/7s\) (actinoid pattern, wrong period), (C) gives 8 electrons beyond \(Xe\) (that is \(Z = 62\), samarium), and (D) is the configuration of cerium. Answer (A).

At S.T.P. one mole of gas occupies \(22400\) mL, so
\[n(O_{2}) = \frac{5600}{22400} = 0.25 \text{ mol}\]
Oxygen is liberated at the anode by
\[2H_{2}O \rightarrow O_{2} + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-}\]
so 1 mol \(O_{2}\) needs 4 mol electrons, and \(0.25\) mol \(O_{2}\) needs \(0.25 \times 4 = 1\) mol electrons.
Silver is deposited by \(Ag^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Ag\), one electron per atom, so 1 mol of electrons deposits 1 mol \(Ag\):
\[m = 1 \times 108 = 108 \text{ g}\]

The data are \([HI] = 0.005, 0.01, 0.02\) mol L\(^{-1}\) with rates \(7.5 \times 10^{-4}, 3.0 \times 10^{-3}, 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\) mol L\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-1}\).
Writing \(\text{rate} = k[HI]^{n}\) and comparing experiments 1 and 2, where the concentration doubles:
\[\frac{3.0 \times 10^{-3}}{7.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 4 = 2^{n} \Rightarrow n = 2\]
Checking with experiments 2 and 3 (concentration doubles again):
\[\frac{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}{3.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 4 = 2^{n} \Rightarrow n = 2\]
The order of the reaction is 2.

Complete combustion of methane:
\[CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \rightarrow CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O\]
Molar mass of \(CO_{2} = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0\) g mol\(^{-1}\), so
\[n(CO_{2}) = \frac{22}{44} = 0.5 \text{ mol}\]
The stoichiometry is 1 : 1, so \(n(CH_{4}) = 0.5\) mol. Molar mass of \(CH_{4} = 12.0 + 4(1.0) = 16.0\) g mol\(^{-1}\):
\[m(CH_{4}) = 0.5 \times 16.0 = 8 \text{ g}\]
authoredSolutions.54:
The expansion is irreversible against a CONSTANT external pressure, so
\[w = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -\left(80 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{Pa}\right)\left(45 - 30\right)\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}} = -1200\ \mathrm{J}\]
(The values of \(n\) and \(T\) are not needed for the work; they only tell us the process is isothermal.)
For an IDEAL gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, and the process is isothermal, so \(\Delta U = 0\). The first law \(\Delta U = q + w\) then gives
\[q = -w = +1200\ \mathrm{J}\]
The amount of heat transferred is 1200 J (absorbed by the gas).
authoredSolutions.55:
3-Methylhex-2-ene is \(CH_{3}-CH=C(CH_{3})-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-CH_{3}\).
With \(HBr\) in the presence of peroxide the addition is free radical (anti-Markovnikov / Kharasch). \(Br^{\bullet}\) adds to whichever alkene carbon leaves the MORE stable radical: adding \(Br\) to C-2 leaves a tertiary radical at C-3, so
\[A = CH_{3}-CHBr-CH(CH_{3})-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-CH_{3}\]
which is 2-bromo-3-methylhexane.
Stereocentres in A:
C-2 carries \(Br,\ H,\ CH_{3}\) and \(CH(CH_{3})C_{3}H_{7}\) - four different groups.
C-3 carries \(CH_{3},\ H,\ CHBrCH_{3}\) and \(CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{3}\) - four different groups.
There are two dissimilar stereocentres, so the molecule cannot be meso and the number of stereoisomers is \(2^{2} = 4\).
authoredSolutions.56:
Test each structure for the three aromaticity requirements: cyclic, fully conjugated (every ring atom \(sp^{2}\)) and \(4n+2\) \(\pi\) electrons in the closed loop.
image27 - the fused bicyclic drawn with the two ring-fusion carbons carrying hydrogens, i.e. \(sp^{3}\). The conjugation is broken at the ring junction, so it is NOT aromatic.
image28 - benzyl-substituted cyclohexene: it contains an intact benzene ring, which is aromatic \((6\pi)\). The isolated cyclohexene double bond does not matter. AROMATIC.
image29 - the indenyl anion: the carbanion carbon becomes \(sp^{2}\) and its lone pair joins the ring system, giving a fully conjugated bicyclic \(10\pi\) system \((4n+2,\ n = 2)\). AROMATIC.
image30 - the dibenzo-fused five-membered heterocycle: the oxygen lone pair completes conjugation across the tricyclic framework and both benzo rings are aromatic. AROMATIC.
Total number of aromatic compounds \(= 3\).
authoredSolutions.57:
A group is meta directing when it WITHDRAWS electron density from the ring by \(-I\) and especially by \(-R\)/\(-M\), destabilising the ortho and para arenium ions more than the meta one. Groups with a lone pair on the atom attached to the ring, or electron-releasing alkyl groups, are ortho/para directing.
Going through the list:
\(-OCH_{3}\): \(+R\), ortho/para
\(-NO_{2}\): strong \(-R,\ -I\), META
\(-CN\): \(-R,\ -I\), META
\(-CH_{3}\): \(+I\)/hyperconjugation, ortho/para
\(-NHCOCH_{3}\): lone pair on N, \(+R\), ortho/para
\(-COR\): \(-R,\ -I\), META
\(-OH\): \(+R\), ortho/para
\(-COOH\): \(-R,\ -I\), META
\(-Cl\): deactivating by \(-I\) but ortho/para directing by \(+R\)
Meta directing groups: \(-NO_{2},\ -CN,\ -COR,\ -COOH\) \(=\) 4.
authoredSolutions.58:
For \(n = 4\) the allowed subshells are \(4s,\ 4p,\ 4d,\ 4f\) (\(l = 0,1,2,3\)). When each is COMPLETELY filled it holds \(2(2l+1)\) electrons:
\[4s = 2,\quad 4p = 6,\quad 4d = 10,\quad 4f = 14\]
\[\text{Total} = 2 + 6 + 10 + 14 = 32\]
In a filled subshell every orbital holds one electron with \(s = +\frac{1}{2}\) and one with \(s = -\frac{1}{2}\), so exactly half of them have \(s = +\frac{1}{2}\):
\[\frac{32}{2} = 16\]

Both species have 14 valence electrons and are isoelectronic with \(N_{2}\).
\(CO\): \(6 + 8 = 14\) electrons; MO configuration \(\sigma 1s^{2}\sigma^{*}1s^{2}\sigma 2s^{2}\sigma^{*}2s^{2}\pi 2p_{x}^{2}\pi 2p_{y}^{2}\sigma 2p_{z}^{2}\), giving \(N_{b} = 10,\ N_{a} = 4\):
\[\text{B.O.} = \frac{10-4}{2} = 3\]
\(NO^{+}\): \(7 + 8 - 1 = 14\) electrons, the same configuration, so B.O. \(= 3\).
Sum of bond orders \(= 3 + 3 = 6\).

Take \(O = -2\), \(H = +1\), \(Cl = -1\), \(F = -1\), \(Ba = +2\) and solve for sulphur.
\(SO_{3}\): \(x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\)
\(H_{2}SO_{3}\): \(2(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +4\) (yes)
\(SOCl_{2}\): \(x + (-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +4\) (yes)
\(SF_{4}\): \(x + 4(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +4\) (yes)

The figure (image34) shows the resonance structures of acrolein, \(CH_{2}=CH-CHO\):
I \(= CH_{2}=CH-CHO\), neutral, no charge separation, every atom with a complete octet.
II \(= {}^{+}CH_{2}-CH=CH-O^{-}\), charge separated, but the NEGATIVE charge sits on the more electronegative oxygen.
III \(= {}^{-}CH_{2}-CH=CH-O^{+}\), charge separated with the negative charge on carbon and the POSITIVE charge on the electronegative oxygen - the least favourable arrangement.
Applying the rules (a neutral structure is more stable than a charge-separated one; among charge-separated structures the one with the negative charge on the more electronegative atom is better), the order is
\[\mathrm{I} > \mathrm{II} > \mathrm{III}\]
which is option (A).

Steam distillation is used precisely for substances that are STEAM VOLATILE and IMMISCIBLE with water. In a mixture of two immiscible liquids each exerts its own vapour pressure independently, so the mixture boils when
\[p_{\text{substance}} + p_{\text{water}} = p_{\text{atmospheric}}\]
which happens BELOW \(100^{\circ}C\). The compound therefore distils over with the steam at a low temperature and escapes thermal decomposition; non-volatile impurities are left behind.
Ordinary and fractional distillation require the components to be miscible and to differ in boiling point; distillation under reduced pressure is for high-boiling liquids that decompose at their normal boiling point. Hence option (D).

A concentration unit varies with temperature only if it is defined using a VOLUME, because the volume of a liquid expands or contracts when heated.
Molarity \(= \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution in L}}\) - contains volume, so it CHANGES with temperature.
Mass percentage \(= \dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}}\times 100\), molality \(= \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}\) and mole fraction \(= \dfrac{n_{A}}{n_{A}+n_{B}}\) are all built from masses and mole numbers only, and mass is temperature independent.
Hence only molarity changes with temperature, option (A).
